World.title: China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018801/China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.content:
Before they were immortals, they were scammers.

That’s the irreverent premise behind “All Wishes Come True!,” a new Chinese animated comedy that has turned a band of mythological figures from Taoist legend into a summer box-office hit.

Released July 18, the film recasts the Eight Immortals — traditionally symbols of people from all walks of life — as con artists who impersonate gods and deceive worshippers before achieving immortality themselves.

In less than a week, the film has grossed more than 370 million yuan ($51 million), becoming the second highest-grossing domestic animated film of 2026 behind “Boonie Bears: The Hidden Protector.” It also holds an 8.3 rating on Chinese review site Douban, the highest among this summer’s new releases.

The film’s biggest twist unfolds in Penglai, a fairyland where gods and humans coexist under a surprisingly modern bureaucracy governed by an immortals management bureau. Deities are assigned temples, evaluated on performance targets, and ranked on giant leaderboards based on the incense offerings they receive.

Unlike traditional tales of the Eight Immortals’ journey toward enlightenment, the film gives the legendary figures a new beginning: they first appear as schemers targeting the riches of Fu, Lu, and Shou, the three deities of fortune, prosperity, and longevity.

Zhongli Quan, traditionally portrayed as a general who became a Taoist immortal, is reimagined as a con artist who leads the group in impersonating deities. Cao Guojiu, traditionally linked to the Song dynasty (960–1279) imperial court, appears as an official in the immortals management bureau.

After taking over a temple, the group finds itself responsible for granting wishes — and eventually becomes known for catching thieves. Their journey later leads to a clash with the war god Yang Jian.

Director Mu Zhengyang said he designed Penglai as a “first-tier megacity,” where gods and humans operate within a modern social system. “At first, audiences should feel that they’re entering a traditional Eastern fairyland. But once inside, it becomes much more like an amusement park,” he told domestic media.

The film’s character-driven approach also extends to its voice performances. Voice director Chen Hao, who worked on the popular “Ne Zha” films, voices Zhongli Quan, while Tieguai Li’s Chongqing dialect adds regional flavor to the character.

The film’s cultural references have also fueled online discussion. On streaming platform Bilibili, videos decoding more than 100 Easter eggs and hidden details have each attracted nearly one million views.

One widely discussed clue is the Eight Immortals’ temple number — 1350, the same number associated with Sun Wukong, better known as the Monkey King, in the “Book of Life and Death,” a mythical register of the underworld in “Journey to the West,” hinting at his possible appearance later in the story.

The same reinterpretation has also drawn criticism from some viewers, who argue that the film alters the identities and values associated with traditional mythology.

Yang Jian, for example, traditionally portrayed as a righteous war god who protects ordinary people, is reimagined as a figure willing to sacrifice heaven and humanity to save his mother. The film’s other redesigns have also drawn attention, including Cao Guojiu’s portrayal as an overweight, flamboyant official and Lan Caihe’s depiction as a toddler.

The debate also extends to the film’s portrayal of immortality. Through the line, “Only immortals can do good deeds,” it offers a new interpretation that some viewers praised, while others argued it differs from traditional Taoist ideas of attaining eternal life.

The production team, based in southwestern China’s Sichuan province, said the Eight Immortals offer creative space for reinterpretation because many audiences know their famous stories but are less familiar with their broader legends. The filmmakers said they hoped to introduce the figures to a new generation through a fresh retelling.

“We didn’t want to simply bring the Eight Immortals in front of young audiences and tell the same story again,” producer Ying Xujun told domestic media. “We had to create something new for a new generation.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A poster for “All Wishes Come True!” From Douban)

World.title: At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.content:
This year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai was larger, more crowded, and more politically prominent than in previous editions.

President Xi Jinping attended the event for the first time, while more than 1,100 companies showcased computing systems, AI agents, robots, and other products aimed at workplaces, factories, and consumers. In-person visits topped 400,000, and tickets were reportedly resold for more than 1,000 yuan.

Xi called for wider access to open-source AI, and China launched a 29-country AI cooperation body, placing issues of governance, access, and international coordination alongside the usual displays of commercial technology.

Beyond the speeches and packed exhibition halls, the most revealing conversations were practical: lowering computing costs, putting AI agents to work, managing new safety risks, and building businesses that can last.

Here are four takeaways from this year’s WAIC.

Computing power gets practical

Computing power was one of the most discussed topics at this year’s WAIC, second only to AI applications by number of related forums. But the focus moved beyond building more data centers or training ever-larger models.

Two questions dominated: what the next generation of computing power might look like, and how to make today’s resources cheaper and more efficient.

At one flagship forum on the future of computing, scientists discussed emerging approaches including quantum computing and space-based computing. Among the speakers was Pan Jianwei, a leading quantum physicist and recent recipient of a top United Nations science award, who outlined recent advances in the field.

Pan also urged caution. Although the field has reached a series of important milestones, he said, building a general-purpose quantum computer capable of quickly solving problems with clear practical value will still require years of sustained research. The academic community, he added, has a responsibility to help the public assess the technology realistically and guard against an industry bubble.

Companies also seemed more focused on improving the efficiency of existing computing resources and reducing the cost of each AI query.

Some were working to improve the performance of models trained mainly on Nvidia chips when deployed on Chinese chips. Others focused on allocating and managing computing resources more efficiently.

Rather than chasing only the most powerful and expensive models, many Chinese AI companies appeared more concerned with making AI cheaper to run.

AI Governance and Safety

AI governance and safety were prominent throughout this year’s WAIC, from high-level forums to the opening ceremony and President Xi Jinping’s speech.

Brian Tse, an AI safety expert and founder and CEO of Concordia AI, said he has seen more discussion in China around cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure, especially the risks posed by frontier AI models.

“The threat landscape is evolving rapidly,” Tse said. “Many experts at the forums expressed concern that threats and potential misuse are developing faster than society’s current defenses.”

The concerns also appeared to be shifting beyond large language models and the harmful content they can generate. More attention was paid this year to the risks posed by autonomous AI agents, which can plan tasks, make decisions, and interact with other tools.

On July 15, just before WAIC, China’s new rules on AI anthropomorphic interaction took effect, targeting services that simulate human personalities and sustained emotional interaction. The rules prohibit providers from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors and bar services from inducing emotional dependence or addiction.

In May, regulators also released guidance on the standardized application and development of AI agents, including plans to explore digital identity management for them.

“China is positioning itself as an architect of multilateral AI governance,” Tse said.

AI lands at work

One phrase heard often at this year’s WAIC was AI’s real-world “landing” — the push to move the technology out of demos and into everyday work. Companies ranging from Tencent and Alibaba to smaller startups showed AI products aimed at offices, factories, and consumer services. AI agents were among the most visible examples.

At booths run by major tech firms, exhibitors demonstrated how agents could be built into corporate workflows, from searching internal documents to generating reports and coordinating routine tasks.

The impact could be broad because many of these companies’ software systems are already embedded in Chinese workplaces. Adding AI agents to existing platforms may prove easier than persuading companies to adopt entirely new tools.

Still, genuinely effective applications appeared limited. Office productivity remained the most obvious use case, while other areas were less developed.

Robotics and embodied AI occupied an entire floor at this year’s WAIC. Visitors could still see robots performing awkward dances or taking six minutes to make a cup of tea. But some companies were beginning to move beyond staged demonstrations, showing robots designed for inspection, manufacturing, logistics, and other industrial uses.

The founder rush

Some of the most revealing conversations at this year’s WAIC took place after the official sessions ended.

Across after-hours gatherings, private meetups, and open-mic sessions, young founders and industry professionals swapped ideas on AI agents, robotics, and productivity tools. Some gatherings ran late into the night, with almost any topic open for discussion.

Many entrepreneurs seemed eager to absorb every new idea, experiment, business opportunity, and professional connection they could find.

But that urgency also carried risks. Some founders said their AI ventures were burning through years of savings. Many still lacked a convincing answer to a basic question: how their projects would generate lasting value and revenue.

That tension ran through WAIC: crowded halls, founders eager to share projects and failures, and a palpable fear of moving too slowly and missing the AI wave. The mood mixed optimism with anxiety, much of it fueled by the speed of the technology and the sheer volume of information surrounding it.

The conversations also suggested a maturing industry. More speakers and founders were asking not only what AI could do, but where it could be useful, how it could be governed, and which businesses could survive once the initial excitement fades.

(Header image: A humanoid robot from a Chinese robotics firm waves Chinese national flags during the 2026 WAIC in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP Photo via VCG)

World.title: The Soybean That Built Northeast China
World.content:
In 2020, I traveled to Kaishantun, a town in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture near the China-North Korea border. It fit every stereotype of the deindustrialized Northeast. Young people had left. The government had built two rows of barracks-style apartment blocks for the elderly residents who remained. Kaishantun railway station had long been abandoned. On the station sign, the space for the next stop was blank. North Korea lay only a few hundred meters away.

On the walk back, I wandered into a derelict movie theater and discovered several reels of old film. Later restored, they revealed something astonishing: clips of a symphony orchestra and a traditional folk orchestra.

What kind of small town could support two orchestras of its own?

As I dug deeper into the history of my home region, Northeast China, I found that part of the answer lay in a crop that today frequently appears in international headlines: soybeans. A century before China became a major importer of American soybeans, it was the world’s leading producer.

In August 1872, three Japanese army officers, disguised as merchants and acting on the orders of General Saigō Takamori, traveled through “Manchuria,” the term they used for Northeast China. Saigō was studying relations between Japan, Korea, and China as he prepared a future campaign against Korea. A year later, the officers submitted their “Report on an Inspection of Manchuria,” one of Japan’s earliest intelligence briefings on China. The report includes a detailed discussion of soybeans:

“From winter through spring, soybeans are continuously transported by inland waterways. Regardless of the cold, day and night, dozens of horse-drawn carts move in a single direction. Large merchants purchase the beans and pile them into circular mountains more than two rooms across and over 6 meters high … The quantity stored is beyond counting.”

In 1885, another Japanese military officer, Kikuchi Setsuzō, passed through Northeast China on his return from the Russian Empire. Along the way, he studied how Qing forces fed their military horses, which he regarded as superior to those of Japan and Russia. Qing troops processed the residue left after soybean oil extraction into pressed soybean cakes for animal feed. Each cake weighed about 12.5 kilograms and could feed three horses for a day. Kikuchi even claimed such soybean resources would be “indispensable” for training military horses.

In the 19th century, Kikuchi was among the few who grasped soybeans’ strategic significance. The crop had reached Europe and North America in the 18th century but remained largely a botanical curiosity. A handful of enthusiasts, such as the Austro-Hungarian agronomist Friedrich Haberlandt, sought to introduce soybeans into Western diets. Yet while they imported the crop, they did not import the culinary traditions that had made it a staple across Asia.

In East Asia, by contrast, people had accumulated more than a thousand years of experience cooking and consuming soybeans. They also recognized the crop’s value as animal feed. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japanese rice farmers gradually abandoned traditional fish-based fertilizers in favor of soybean cake. Between 1882 and 1902, Japan’s soybean imports increased four-hundredfold.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 finally alerted the world to soybeans’ importance. European military observers noted that both sides relied heavily on the crop. Japanese forces consumed soybeans directly and used them in military logistics. Russian forces fed them to cavalry horses. Soybean oil served as a raw material for soap and as a lubricant for artillery equipment and wagon axles.

The soybean trade expanded rapidly. A 1911 report from the Customs Service in Shanghai observed that “It is only in the last three years that soya beans have become important in intercontinental commerce,” calling their rapid emergence from obscurity “one of the most remarkable commercial events of recent times.” In the same year, the U.S. ambassador in Beijing told the State Department that Northeast China had until recently been largely unknown for its commercial potential, despite supplying soybeans to global markets. He observed that its economic trajectory was now drawing attention in major cities including New York, London, Hamburg, and Seattle, and attributed this shift to soybeans, whose rapidly growing demand he characterized as “phenomenal in trade annals.”

Estimates suggest that Northeast China accounted for between 16% and 42% of global soybean production between 1908 and 1930, shipping soybeans, soybean oil, and soybean cakes to the rest of China, Japan, and Europe. Until the eve of World War II, China produced more than 80% of the world’s soybeans. The crop became widely known as the “Manchurian bean.”

Soybeans were also among the most important exports of a then largely impoverished China. After World War I, their importance grew rapidly, and by the 1920s they had overtaken tea and silk to become China’s leading export, accounting for more than 20% of export earnings.

As trade expanded, so did Japan’s territorial ambitions. In the run-up to Japan's formal annexation of Korea in 1910, Yanbian became a frontier along the China-Korea border where Chinese and Japanese spheres of influence met directly. Japanese strategists viewed the wider Yanbian area as a gateway to the interior of Northeast China and sought to build a railway linking the Korean port of Chongjin with China’s inland Northeast. General Hasegawa Yoshimichi, commander of Japanese forces in Korea, regarded Yanbian as a vital supply corridor for sustaining colonial rule on the peninsula. He advocated occupying the region to secure access to strategic commodities such as soybeans.

Over the following three decades, Japan steadily expanded its influence in Northeast China. In 1931, Japanese forces seized the region and took control of its economic resources. This expansion, justified in the name of protecting economic “lifelines,” would later extend across Asia during the Pacific War to the oil fields of Burma, Sumatra, and Borneo; the rubber plantations of Malaya; and the chromium and iron deposits of the Philippines.

In Yanbian, war and colonial rule only reinforced the region’s economic importance. Beyond soybeans, Japanese authorities coveted the region’s timber. In Kaishantun they established the Eastern Manchuria Rayon Pulp Company, whose output eventually surpassed that of most producers in Japan. After the Chinese Communist Party won the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949, the new state’s flagship pulp and paper enterprise was established in the same town.

Factories brought more than jobs. They brought hospitals, movie theaters, and even symphony orchestras.

Yet by then Northeast China was no longer the sole center of the global soybean trade. By the early 20th century, American farmers were already familiar with soybeans, using them to replenish soil and support other crops. After the Russo-Japanese War, however, the crop’s industrial potential attracted growing attention.

One unlikely champion was Henry Ford. He used soybean protein and soybean-oil derivatives in automotive components and in 1941 unveiled a prototype car with body panels made largely from soybean-based plastic. To demonstrate its strength, he famously struck it with an axe.

Ford’s soybean car was hardly a commercial success, but it generated publicity for the crop. When Japan severed America’s access to Asian supply routes during the Pacific War, soybeans were transformed from an industrial curiosity into a strategic resource. Combined harvesters and advances in plant breeding helped American farmers scale up production.

By the 1950s, the center of gravity in soybean production had shifted decisively to the Americas.

One final piece was still missing from the modern soybean map: Brazil. In the early 1970s, a major El Niño event, a climate pattern that warms the Pacific Ocean, devastated the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, a key source of animal feed, driving demand for soybean meal. Prices surged, and in 1973 the Nixon administration imposed restrictions on soybean exports.

History then took an ironic turn. Japan, heavily dependent on imported American soybeans, increased its investment in South American agriculture, while Brazil’s agricultural research agency, Embrapa, developed soybean varieties suited to tropical conditions. The result was a dramatic expansion of Brazilian production.

In 2024, more than 70% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil. When trade tensions between China and the United States intensified in 2025, Brazil became China’s principal alternative for former U.S. suppliers.

Northeast China remains the country’s most important soybean-growing region, producing the beans that become tofu and soy milk on Chinese tables. But it no longer supplies the world with soybean oil and soybean meal. Once-thriving industrial towns have been swept up in the tide of deindustrialization, leaving behind abandoned railway stations and empty movie theaters.

From an unassuming plant in Northeast China to one of the world’s most traded agricultural commodities, the soybean’s history is ultimately a story of globalization. A soybean harvested in Paraguay may be processed in Argentina, sold to China by a trading house in Geneva, and eventually find its way into milk, cakes, or meat products. It shapes what we eat, how we farm, and how nations interact with one another. It also shapes the fate of countless small towns, including places like Kaishantun.

(Header image: A soybean field in Xingkai Lake Farm, Heilongjiang province, 2023. VCG)

World.title: This Filipino physicist brings outer space closer to home
World.content:
When Dr. Gay Jane Perez was a kid, she never thought that she would grow up to be a decorated physicist, a postdoctoral fellow at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), a leader in the space economy, as well as the director general of the Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA).

“Although much, much younger, I did think about being an astronaut. But not so seriously, just in a way that was, ‘Oh! It would be cool to be an astronaut! I want to be an astronaut.’ But what course would you take to be an astronaut? There’s no Filipino astronaut,” she shared. “So it’s just one of those things that will cross your mind but you don’t have a pathway to get it.”

Perez didn’t even attend a science high school. As a student of the Universidad de Santa Isabel in Naga City, she grew up seeing lawyers, accountants, and doctors at career fairs, not scientists. Her school also focused on developing well-rounded leaders, writers, and public speakers.

Even if she was an active student leader herself, she felt like those skills were her weaknesses, so she gravitated to math instead of words. While her friends were winning extemporaneous speaking competitions, she was winning math olympiads.

She chose to major in physics — the science with the most math, she thought then — at the University of the Philippines (UP) Diliman after the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) offered a scholarship and incentivized the science course.

But while her strength in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) gave her an edge among her high school classmates, all her college peers came from science high schools. She struggled to keep up after everything she knew about physics was covered in the first week.

To her surprise, her perceived weaknesses became her strengths. While applying for a prestigious research lab in her third year of college, her lecture and presentation on the science behind the animation technology of Toy Story captured the attention of her audience.

“Before me, people were chatting during the other presentations. But when I started giving my talk, they all started listening, including the head of the lab, Dr. Caesar Saloma, who eventually became my advisor,” she recalled.

“I guess it turned out that they’re not used to hearing somebody like me. My weakness when I was in high school was my strength when I was in college because I’m more comfortable speaking in front of the class, more than the rest. But it’s all relative, right? So, I thought, if they only knew my high school friends!”

That moment was transformative, especially for a struggling Perez, who was just trying to pass her subjects.

“They must have seen my potential and decided to bet on me, even if I wasn’t as good as those from the science high schools,” she said. “So when they accepted me, I valued it immensely, especially since I ended up doing really well on the research part. I super enjoyed the act of research! Exploring something that you don’t know where it will lead to… I found it very interesting and exciting because every day is unique.”

Mission: Come back home

It was also in college that she found the role models in the sciences that she didn’t have growing up. One of the most influential to her was Saloma, former chancellor of UP Diliman and professor emeritus at the National Institute of Physics.

“He’s the one that really expressed passion for science, and more importantly, doing science in the Philippines. We had some scientists before in the Philippines who are now celebrated scientists out of the country. A few chose to stay and continue to do the science here, and he is one of them,” she said.

“But what I learned from him, which influenced me in my career, is that you can do science in the Philippines and you are most needed here. You can create the highest impact here because the science that you do will help our society.”

ROLE MODEL. Dr. Gay Jane Perez sends a message of inspiration for the high school participants of CanSat 101, a program for hands-on satellite development through the CanSat model. Photo courtesy of PhilSA

After she was accepted into a postdoctoral fellowship at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, she took with her those lessons from Saloma all the way to Washington, DC. Even when immersed in a world-class research center with top-of-the-line equipment at her disposal and Nobel Prize winning scientists down the hall from her office, she never forgot the Philippines.

Throughout her time in NASA, she found herself constantly thinking, “How I wish we have something similar in the Philippines. I want to bring this to the Philippines.” After just a few months, she couldn’t wait to go back home.

At that time, many people were awaiting her return home and counting on her contributions to the country. She made a parallel about how she felt back then in NASA when Christina Koch of the Artemis II mission became the first woman to orbit around the moon.

“During their final burn to go to the moon, the last statement [Koch] said was, ‘We choose Earth.’ So, for me, it was like I went to NASA on a mission to come back home,” Perez said.

NASA on Philippine soil

Back in the Philippines, she applied the research she conducted and data she gathered in NASA by leading the development of the Philippines’ first local microsatellite, Diwata-1, and launched it in 2016. The satellite data was used for drought forecasting, agricultural monitoring, and climate assessment, targeted toward serving farmers and the agricultural sector during intense seasons of El Niño.

Perez, although already a decorated scientist at this point, had a dream she still wanted to fulfill: to have something like NASA on Philippine soil.

The next step was a no-brainer for the scientist as she eventually contributed to the establishment of the Philippine Space Agency. She had first served as officer-in-charge, deputy director general, and finally appointed director general by President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. in January 2026.

LEADER. Dr. Gay Jane Perez takes her oath as director general of PhilSA in January 2026. Photo from Perez’s LinkedIn

As a six-year old government agency, PhilSA is young, new, and exciting. Perez shared that the agency is now 247 personnel strong. Having been involved in its formation since Day 1, she knows that its people are the most crucial in ensuring its effectiveness and sustainability.

But with “brain drain” — Filipino scientists choosing to migrate to countries with better pay, conditions, and research opportunities — the challenge is not to ask them to stay, but to create an environment that makes them want to stay.

“What we are striving for and we think is really necessary is to create the environment for them to thrive, to absorb them. Because otherwise, the same narrative of a Filipino who eventually will seek for greener pastures out of the country, or will find more meaningful things to do outside, will continue,” Perez said.

“[They usually think,] ‘What can I do here? We don’t have the equipment, we don’t have the resources, I’m better off doing my science outside, elsewhere.’ So creating that environment where they can see that they will thrive and excel and do good and do meaningful and impactful science, that’s still a work in progress. Now, in my capacity as the head of the agency, that’s where I’m focusing my energy.”

The Philippine scientific community is resourceful and adaptable amid the lack of funding, equipment, and working “against all odds.” But Perez isn’t one to romanticize struggle. For her, pursuing a career in science shouldn’t always come with so many roadblocks.

The organization’s annual Philippine Space Week is one way they are able to present to stakeholders and the general public why it is worth investing and betting on PhilSA and the Philippine scientific community.

Throughout the week, they present the breakthroughs they achieved that year, the people and partnerships who made it all possible, and the emerging possibilities and opportunities that the space economy has to offer. They also show the problems and issues that space technology and data can help solve and the ways they can be implemented to serve the Filipino people.

Through this event, they not only show what science in the Philippines can achieve, but also why scientists in the country are needed and worth supporting.

Discoveries, adventures

If, growing up, Perez never had a scientist speak at her career fair, it was a full circle moment for her to get invited to be her high school’s commencement speaker. She has now become the role model she never had in her formative years. Now, she’s dedicated herself to showing others that a career in the sciences is full of exciting discoveries and adventures.

“They also used to say that becoming a scientist is like a vow of poverty, that you won’t get rich from the sciences. But I think that is not fair,” Perez said. “It is true in the sense that you won’t get rich, but it’s not like it will make you poor. And while you won’t get rich because you don’t get a lot of money, maybe you don’t need that much, anyway.”

LESSONS. Dr. Gay Jane Perez delivers a talk at the 2026 Annual Philippine-American Academy of Science and Engineering (PAASE) Meeting and Symposium in Bagac, Bataan. Photo from Perez’s LinkedIn

“I also think it’s a very decent and high integrity profession,” Perez added. “Because for one, you disincentivize lying. Because science, right? You need data, facts. So this is a profession where you can earn by simply telling the truth. You can sleep soundly at night.”

To the young Filipinos who are considering a career in the sciences, she wants them to know that, “There’s a future for you here. I’m one of you. Like you, before, I didn’t see a clear [career] path in the sciences. But now you can see me.” – Rappler.com

Quotes in Filipino were translated to English for brevity.

Elise Suarez is a Rappler intern from Puerto Princesa City and a Humanities student of the University of Asia & the Pacific.

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s SONA 2026
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is set to deliver his State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27, 4 pm, at the Batasang Pambansa in Quezon City.

The situation is markedly different from last year, when Marcos’ erstwhile ally, Vice President Sara Duterte, avoided an impeachment trial after the Supreme Court ruled that the complaint against her was unconstitutional as it is barred by the one-year rule.

This year, as Marcos delivers his fifth SONA, the impeachment trial against the Vice President is in full swing. Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez, the President’s cousin, is no longer House speaker following his resignation after he was implicated in flood control corruption. Marcos himself had announced a crackdown on those involved in the scandal in his SONA last year.

How will Marcos set the tone for the last two years of his presidency? What promises will he declare as fulfilled, and what remains to be done? What will be his new marching order a year since he called for a crackdown on flood control corruption?

Bookmark and refresh this page for updates, analyses, fact checks, and videos as Marcos delivers his fifth SONA.

World.title: No go for Alex Eala-Venus Williams doubles pairing in Washington Open
World.content:
EAGER. The Philippines' Alexandra Eala reacts during her third-round match against Poland's Iga Swiatek in the 2026 Wimbledon Championships.

Alex Eala will instead focus on singles action as she battles Asian Games tormentor Zheng Qinwen of China in the opening round of the Washington Open

MANILA, Philippines – Plans for a repeat team-up between Alex Eala and tennis icon Venus Williams have fallen through.

The Filipina will instead focus on singles action of the Washington Open in the United States as Williams partners with fellow American Diana Shnaider in doubles play.

Eala and Williams were announced as doubles partners by the WTA 500 tournament and even practiced together days before the start of the competition, but the draw released on Saturday, July 25, showed otherwise.

The development derailed aspirations for Eala and Williams to go on a deeper run after they joined forces for the first time and reached the quarterfinals of the Bad Homburg Open in Germany in June.

Eala opens her singles campaign against China’s Zheng Qinwen in the round of 32 as the two Asian bets meet on the WTA Tour for the first time.

But Eala and Zheng are familiar with each other — the Chinese former world No. 4 beating the Filipina in the semifinals of the 2022 Asian Games on the way to winning the gold medal.

A lot has changed, though, since as Eala now ranks No. 29 in the world while Zheng sits outside the top 100 at No. 123.

Eala is coming off a warm homecoming, where she was honored by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and warmly welcomed by fans.

The 21-year-old hopes to build on the momentum from her splendid grass-court campaign that she capped with a historic run to the fourth round of the Wimbledon Championships as she begins the hard-court swing in Washington. – Rappler.com

World.title: [ANALYSIS] Marcos’ shrinking influence in the legislative
World.content:
The two men seated behind him during the 2025 SONA won't make a comeback on that stage this year. It's a testament to the political upheaval that has reshaped both chambers of Congress over the past year.

When President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers his fourth State of the Nation Address (SONA) in end-July, he will face a legislative branch that has gone through turmoil in the past year, and he will continue to grapple with his waning — and sometimes underutilized — influence.

On the surface, Congress’ turnaround rate on Marcos’ pet bills this year doesn’t paint a flattering picture. Excluding his inaugural SONA in 2022, this will be the first time he takes the podium with only one priority measure enacted that he can point to as an accomplishment.

That means that out of 52 bills identified as a priority by the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council, only one — the resetting of the Bangsamoro elections — was signed into law.

That is unlike in previous years, when anywhere from six to 21 pet bills hurdled the legislative branch by the time of his address to the Filipino public. The SONA, after all, is the biggest stage to tout the achievements of his administration.

To be fair to Marcos, the legislative grind typically slows after the midterm elections, as a newly constituted Congress regroups and reassesses which priority bills are worth pushing to the finish line before the next elections usher in the President’s successor.

For the part of the House, whose majority leader is no less than his son Sandro Marcos, 20 out of 51 pending pet bills hurdled the chamber in the past year, but all of them got stuck at the Senate.

The low productivity rate at the upper chamber, however, stems from an unprecedented episode of chaos that Marcos was slow to contain.

Senate

The holdup of bills at the upper chamber took place under the short-lived but destructive Senate presidency of Alan Peter Cayetano.

Virtually no legislative work was accomplished — no anti-dynasty bill, no freedom of information measure, not even the proposed abolition of the travel tax, a relatively easy win that could have earned Marcos goodwill among middle-class voters.

During Cayetano’s weeks-long rule, triggered by a surprise coup, a gun fight broke out inside Senate premises, fugitive Bato dela Rosa escaped from Senate custody, the minority walked out from the session hall in protest, and Cayetano’s majority boycotted the session.

Play Video

It is uncommon in Philippine politics for the Senate president to be a rival of the President, but that’s what Cayetano has been for Marcos.

The President’s recent challenges in keeping the Senate on his side have hardly been a surprise. His slate’s underperformance during the midterms — seen as a referendum on his presidency — resulted in more Duterte-allied politicians winning Senate seats instead of survey-favored administration candidates.

The consequence is an aggressive Senate bloc ready to platform former bodyguards who claimed that top officials, including Marcos, received billions of pesos in kickbacks from public works projects.

The Senate minority now has 11 members, a stark contrast from the two-member minority during the first half of the Marcos administration.

House

Malacañang’s logic has been straightforward: Marcos was the one who exposed flood control anomalies during his SONA last year, so he would not be dumb enough to do that if his hands were not clean.

During that address, he uttered one of the punchiest soundbites of his presidency — “Mahiya naman kayo!” — an emotional warning against people who manipulate the budget for their personal gain.

Play Video

The two men seated behind him at the time suffered the consequences of the scandal: then-Senate president Chiz Escudero for the campaign donation he received from a top contractor in his province, and then-House speaker Martin Romualdez for his role in the passage of what critics described as “mangled” 2025 national budget.

Cousin Romualdez, until his resignation last year, was an effective and efficient ally of the President. Congressmen had little to no complaints, funding poured in for their districts, most of Malacañang’s pet bills cleared the lower chamber, and one of them — the Maharlika Investment Fund — even passed in record time during the early years of the Marcos administration. Romualdez had the ears of the President, he was a companion to Marcos’ foreign trips, and he rallied the troops to impeach Vice President Sara Duterte for the first time in 2025, even if Marcos publicly insisted he had nothing to do with it.

Romualdez’s successor Bojie Dy came from northern Luzon, a bailiwick of the Marcoses. While he is a party mate of the President, the strength of his ties to the President cannot match what the cousins had.

Months into his post, Dy had to contend with growing dissatisfaction from the House’s second-largest bloc, the National Unity Party, which blamed the executive for bottlenecks in the release of district funds, and Dy for failing to effectively press Malacañang to address their concerns.

Privately, some lawmakers, while insisting they had done nothing wrong, also bristled at Marcos’ SONA callout, saying it placed their actions under intense public scrutiny.

The House, however, is still unlikely to turn its back on the President. Earlier this year, it swiftly dismissed an impeachment complaint against Marcos over his alleged involvement in the budget kickback scheme.

Even so, his administration will continue to contend with outspoken lawmakers eager to seize on any perceived misstep — from figures such as Leandro Leviste and Edgar Erice to the Duterte bloc and the usual voices from the traditional opposition.

Marcos is entering the lame-duck phase of his presidency, and the next two years will test whatever political capital he has left: first, whether he can marshal enough support to secure the conviction of a vice president out for blood, despite his apparent reluctance to acknowledge that her permanent disqualification would bolster his family’s political future; and second, whether he can persuade Congress to pass key bills that will ultimately define his legacy. – Rappler.com

World.title: Marcos promised a crackdown on flood control corruption. What happened a year later?
World.content:
While hundreds of millions of pesos have been recovered, that amount is still only a fraction of the estimated losses

A year ago, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. vowed to prosecute everyone involved in corruption in flood control projects.

“Sa mga susunod na buwan, makakasuhan ang lahat ng mga lalabas na may sala mula sa imbestigasyon. Pati na ang mga kasabwat na kontratista sa buong bansa,” Marcos said in his fourth State of the Nation Address on July 28, 2025.

(In the coming months, we will file charges against those found at fault. Including their accomplices, contractors all over the country.)

“Mahiya naman kayo sa kapwa ‘nyo Pilipino,” he said. (Feel some shame toward your fellow Filipinos!)

One year later, cases have been filed against at least 30 individuals in different courts. At least 24 are officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). The list also includes Senator Jinggoy Estrada and former senator Bong Revilla.

Most of those facing cases have been detained. Former Ako Bicol representative Zaldy Co — linked to several construction companies — remains at large.

The scandal, however, has extended far beyond those formally charged.

Rappler’s investigation found that some members of the Marcos Cabinet, dozens of House members, and local officials — from mayors and vice mayors to councilors — also served as government contractors, securing multimillion-peso infrastructure projects and raising questions about conflicts of interest.

Even the President’s cousin, Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez was implicated, prompting him to resign as speaker. The Office of the Ombudsman described him as “the central figure in a scheme built on the diversion of public funds meant for flood control projects.”

Former budget secretary Amenah Pangandaman also resigned after being implicated in the alleged budget manipulation that enabled millions of pesos in public funds to be diverted. In July, she was appointed chair and chief executive officer of the state-run Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank.

The flood control corruption controversy sparked nationwide protests, with thousands of Filipinos taking to the streets. Some demonstrations also called for Marcos’ resignation.

Both the House of Representatives and the Senate launched investigations into the alleged anomalies. The House inquiry, however, ended after only a few hearings, after lawmakers said the probe would give way to a new investigation commission created by Marcos. The House-led probe had itself come under scrutiny because dozens of lawmakers allegedly had ties to government contractors or were contractors themselves.

The congressional investigations also implicated legislators, including senators and members of the House.

Even then-public works secretary Manuel Bonoan became embroiled in the controversy. Under his watch, a construction firm linked to his daughter secured about P2.5-billion worth of DPWH contracts. Bonoan later resigned. Bonoan is now under hospital arrest.

Money lost

No one knows exactly how much public money was lost to flood control corruption.

Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson has estimated that about 60% of the country’s flood control budget had been pocketed.

MONEY. Wads of cash inside a house within the perimeters of the DPWH Bulacan 1st DEO, as shown by whistleblower Engineer Brice Gonzalez to the House of Representatives on September 9, 2025.

Over the past 15 years, the government has allocated more than P1.9 trillion for flood control projects under the DPWH. By Lacson’s estimate, that translates to roughly P1.14 trillion lost to corruption.

So far, authorities have recovered only P611.379 million from individuals linked to the scheme, including:

DPWH Undersecretary Roberto Bernardo – P290 million

DPWH Bulacan District Engineer Henry Alcantara – P180.379 million

DPWH NCR District Engineer Gerard Opulencia – P120 million

Contractor Sally Santos – P20 million

The Anti-Money Laundering Council Bank also froze the assets of officials linked to the flood control corruption mess.

The investigation also revealed how millions of pesos stacked on tables were divided among DPWH engineers, among others, and cash packed into suitcases for delivery to politicians.

Meanwhile, social media users highlighted the lavish lifestyles of nepo babies or the children of contractors and other personalities linked to the scandal. Some DPWH engineers from Bulacan also burned millions of pesos in casinos, as exposed by Senator Ping Lacson in a privilege speech.

Clean up

To clean up the corruption-plagued DPWH, Marcos appointed one of his closest allies, former transportation secretary Vince Dizon, to lead the agency.

On his first day in office on September 1, 2025, Dizon ordered the “unqualified courtesy resignation” of all incumbent undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, regional directors, bureau directors, service directors, project directors, and district engineers.

He then traveled across the country inspecting flood control projects, eventually identifying dozens of alleged ghost and substandard projects. According to Dizon, government agencies had uncovered at least 421 ghost flood control projects nationwide.

FLOOD CONTROL. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. inspects a flood control project in Baliwag City, Bulacan, on August 20, 2025.

The administration also launched a public reporting portal for suspected anomalous projects. Within less than a month, it received at least 12,000 complaints.

Marcos also created the Independent Commission for Infrastructure to investigate not only flood control anomalies, but also other major infrastructure projects over the previous decade.

The commission operated for only six months, after saying that its job was done.

Its three-member panel gradually unraveled. Former DPWH secretary Rogelio “Babes” Singson resigned first. Weeks later, Rossana Fajardo also stepped down, leaving only the commission’s chairman Andres Reyes Jr.

Throughout its brief existence, the commission faced criticism over its limited powers, lack of resources and transparency, and questions about its independence. Even Singson publicly questioned whether it had the authority needed to fulfill its mandate.

Before effectively ceasing operations, the commission turned over its findings to the Office of the Ombudsman.

Budget reforms

The scandal also reshaped the national budget process.

The House abolished its so-called “small committee,” a powerful group of lawmakers that traditionally handled individual amendments even after the proposed budget had passed second reading.

For the first time, bicameral conference committee deliberations were livestreamed, giving the public a rare glimpse into negotiations that had long taken place behind closed doors.

The House also launched a public budget website aimed at making appropriations more transparent.

Meanwhile, under Dizon, the DPWH removed P252-billion worth of locally-funded flood control projects from its proposed 2026 budget.

Congress is set to deliberate the 2027 national budget next.

While hundreds of millions of pesos have been recovered, that amount is still only a fraction of the estimated losses. And while dozens are facing cases, many other officials implicated in the controversy continue to hold public office.

With only two years left, can Marcos really get to the bottom of this multi-billion corruption scheme? – Rappler.com

World.title: Can SONA 2026 be a ‘pivotal moment’ for Marcos?
World.content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr delivers his 4th State of the Nation Address, at the House of Representatives, on July 28, 2025.

Alliance of Concerned Teachers vice chairperson Carl Marc Ramota says President Marcos' fifth SONA is a chance for him 'to present a clear, citizen-centered roadmap that favors solutions over feuds'

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27, can be a chance for him to restore public trust that has steadily eroded over the last four years, but it won’t be an easy task.

“The upcoming [SONA] is a pivotal moment. A chance to present a clear, citizen-centered roadmap that favors solutions over feuds,” Alliance of Concerned Teachers vice chairperson Carl Marc Ramota said at the Center for People Empowerment in Governance’s (CenPEG) 2026 State of the Presidency Forum held at the University of the Philippines on July 21.

“If the President can steer the ship back to these fundamentals — accountability, economic relief, and governance — the tide of public trust can return,” Ramota added.

Four years into his term, Marcos’ public trust score continued to decline. According to the Social Weather Stations’ June 2026 survey, only 34% of Filipinos expressed “much trust” in the President, while Vice President Sara Duterte maintained a 57% trust rating.

With the Constitution declaring that “public office is a public trust,” Ramota said that the ship of state can only sail as far as public confidence in government will carry it.

“In a democracy, sentiment is not whispered in Palace halls. It is measured, broadcasted, and even quantified,” he said. “A leader may survive on bad policy, but if the foundation of trust crumbles, the whole house can collapse.”

‘Kitchen table realities’

One of the victories being trumpeted by the Marcos administration is the Philippines achieving “upper middle income economy” status. While this mirroes decades of “accumulated growth, resilience of remittances, and dynamism of services,” economist Emmanuel Leyco said it does not reflect the realities of many Filipinos.

Ordinary citizens continue to bear the brunt of the economic struggles the country faces, such as the inflating prices of basic goods and services.

“Surveys show that classes D and E, our mass market and poorest sectors, have been the hardest hit. They hold the President directly accountable for their kitchen table realities,” Ramota said.

Leyco said that these sectors suffer even more than the national inflation figures suggest, making the burden of inflation unequal.

“[T]he administration has conceded that affordable living is an objective, not yet a condition. And let me say this: The P20-[rice per kilo] window truly exists and it deserves defending, but the P20-economy does not yet exist and the fifth SONA should plainly say so,” Leyco said.

Filipino already reeling from high prices of basic commodities and fuel are also confronted with questionable multibillion-peso flood control projects, corruption, and the slow process of holding public officials accountable, said Ramota.

He said his created a perception that the government is more concerned with protecting itself than addressing the problems within its own ranks, fueling rising frustration among the people.

The public has witnessed Senate coups, budget disputes, and impeachment proceedings unfold, but these political developments have brought little change to their everyday lives.

Ramota said accountability is expected to become a defining issue ahead of the 2028 elections. The Vice President’s impeachment trial is already influencing the position of political figures ahead of the next race.

“Noise without solutions breeds fatigue, and fatigue morphs into distrust,” he added.

Kabataan Representative Renee Co said the impeachment trial outcome will ultimately determine the level of accountability that can be imposed on public officials involved in corruption. – Patricia Fontilar/Rappler.com

Patricia Fontilar is a journalism student at the University of the Philippines Diliman and the managing editor of Tinig ng Plaridel, the official student publication of the UP College of Media and Communication. She is currently a Rappler intern.

World.title: Rescuers scour South China Sea for 23 missing after Vietnamese vessel sinks
World.content:
Hainan authorities say the cargo vessel Khoi Nguyen 18, with 62 Vietnamese nationals aboard, ran into distress in waters near Fiery Cross Reef, according to a CCTV report

HONG KONG – Rescuers were searching on Sunday, July 26, for 23 people missing after a Vietnamese ship sank in the busy waterway of the South China Sea, while 39 were pulled from the waters, China’s state broadcaster CCTV said.

Authorities in the southern province of Hainan said the cargo vessel Khoi Nguyen 18, with 62 Vietnamese nationals aboard, ran into distress in waters near Fiery Cross Reef, CCTV added.

A distress flare from the vessel was first spotted by a Chinese rescue ship, the Nanhai Jiu 115, on Saturday evening, CCTV said.

Six Chinese vessels, a rescue helicopter, and a Vietnamese vessel joined the search and rescue effort at the site, it said.

The Vietnamese-registered vessel is nearly 70 m (230 ft) long with a gross tonnage of 999 tons.

The area around the reef is part of the disputed Spratly Islands, which China calls the Nansha Islands, a group of highly contested reefs, islets, and atolls in the resource-rich South China Sea.

China claims sovereignty over almost the entire strategic waterway, including the Spratlys, where it has built runways and militarised artificial islands.

But Beijing’s sweeping claims overlap with those of Vietnam, the Philippines, Taiwan, Malaysia, and Brunei. – Rappler.com

World.title: Keeper of Ivatan memory: Dorian Merina sees Batanes beyond the postcard view
World.content:
'Over and over we, as Ivatans, have had to assert our identity and protect our community,' says author Dorian Merina amid recent territorial claims over Batanes by Chinese scholars

While Batanes has long captivated Filipinos with its rolling hills, stone villages, and dramatic coastlines, it’s also an ancestral homeland etched with generations of Ivatan memories — stories that author Dorian Merina has dedicated his life to preserving.

Merina has devoted years documenting indigenous oral poetry and safeguarding traditions that have been passed down through Ivatan communities in this northernmost province, separated from the rest of the country by the Balintang Channel.

An Ivatan himself, Merina’s critically acclaimed book, Di Achichúk, earned the 2020 Gintong Aklat Award and is considered one of the most celebrated literary works to emerge from Batanes in recent years.

Di Achichúk: Poems and Images from Batanes serves as a portrait of Ivatan life, weaving together the islands’ geography, history, language, and lived experiences into a collection of poems.

“I am seeking to share and reflect daily and communal life in Batanes. An important aspect of this is recognizing that, as Ivatans, we are inseparable from the land and our history,” Merina told Rappler.

“We do not regard our place, whether it is our particular village or community, as merely a setting, or a background. The land, the ocean, even a specific hillside, mountain ridge or lagoon, is intricately linked to our memories and experiences.”

Those became even more significant after a group of Chinese scholars revived territorial claims over Batanes.

During an academic symposium held on June 30, 2026, at Jinan University in Guangzhou, China, scholars from institutions including the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and Nanjing University argued that the Batanes and Babuyan island groups are a “natural geographical extension” of Taiwan.

Because Beijing claims sovereignty over Taiwan, they contended that Batanes should also be considered part of China.

Among their arguments was that post-World War II treaties requiring Japan to return occupied territories to China should have included Batanes. They also claimed that the 1898 Treaty of Paris placed the islands outside the territory ceded to the Philippines.

The claims ignored the centuries-long relationship between the Ivatan people and their homeland, said Merina.

“Our families have lived here for many generations,” said Merina, who lives in Savidug, Sabtang, where he helps document and preserve the Ivatan oral poetry tradition known as Laji.

“Our language has evolved in this landscape. These are important distinctions because this understanding automatically engenders a deeper relationship with Batanes and a responsibility to protect its well-being.”

“For many generations, outsiders have tried to redefine, conquer or reshape Batanes. Today, powerful political forces in our region continue this impulse.”

The assertions drew condemnation from Philippine historians, legal experts, and government agencies, all of whom stressed that Batanes has long been recognized as an integral and sovereign part of the Philippines under international law.

The National Historical Commission of the Philippines rejected the scholars’ arguments, pointing to more than a century of historical and scientific evidence.

It noted that Spain formally incorporated Batanes into the Philippine colony in 1783, that British explorer William Dampier found no evidence of Chinese governance when he visited the islands in 1687, and that oceanographic studies show Batanes sits on the continental shelf extending from Northern Luzon rather than Taiwan.

For Merina, however, defending Batanes begins with ensuring that future generations of Ivatans continue to tell their own stories, going beyond historical documents and political statements.

He believes literature and language remain among the strongest forms of cultural resistance, allowing communities to preserve their history and identity.

“Over and over we, as Ivatans, have had to assert our identity and protect our community,” he said.

“Sometimes that comes by strengthening our solidarity with other tribal people in the region or throughout the Philippines. The more we can tell our own stories, preserve our histories and foster our own literature and language, the more we maintain the ability to continue to resist these attempts to take away our autonomy.”



Author Dorian Merina (left) and his book, Di Achichúk, featuring Ivatan life.

Merina also organized community libraries, storytelling sessions, and poetry performances across Batanes to encourage younger Ivatans to reconnect with their language and heritage before these traditions fade.

For him, preserving culture is a personal responsibility owed to both ancestors and future generations.

“This is to provide context and knowledge, and to provoke emotional connection to our tribal history. This is my aim today: to ensure that our place as Ivatans is not erased; but remains strong and resilient for many generations to come,” he said.

Ultimately, Merina hopes Di Achichúk will encourage readers outside Batanes to see the islands for what they are, beyond their breathtaking scenery or geopolitical stance.

He hopes they come to understand the lives, histories, and traditions that have shaped the people who call the islands home.

“This is where literature and stories can make a difference,” Merina said.

“Literature encourages us to learn from each other and understand how events, circumstances, and historical influences are all deeply related. A vacant landscape is much easier to destroy. But a land filled with plants, animals, people and cultural memory is rich in value, and much more resistant to threats.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Last Mile Schools Act seen as lifeline for Zambo del Sur’s remote learners
World.content:
Zamboanga del Sur 1st District Rep. Joseph Kim Yu visits Pisompongan Integrated School in Barangay Pisompongan, Midsalip town, one of the identified last mile schools in Zamboanga del Sur. (Photo from Yu’s social media page)

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur — In the rugged uplands and coastal sitios of Zamboanga del Sur, where children often walk for hours on foot to reach the nearest classroom, a new law promises to change the learning landscape.

Republic Act 12321, or the Last Mile and Geographically Isolated and Disadvantaged Areas (GIDA) Schools Act, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on July 22, institutionalizes government support to upgrade public schools in the country’s most underserved communities.

Zamboanga del Sur 1st District Rep. Joseph Kim Yu co-authored the law and supported its passage in the House of Representatives.

Article continues after this 

During his sponsorship speech for House Bill 1820 before the Committee on Basic Education and Culture last year, Yu painted a vivid picture of the struggles faced by students in his province’s remote barangays.

“Our dear Filipino children are forced to face the hard realities of life, just to obtain the education they deserve,” he said, stressing the urgency of building schools in geographically isolated and conflict-affected areas.

The law mandates the construction of proper classrooms, provision of electricity and clean water, connecting roads, and internet access for last-mile schools.

It also grants teachers in GIDA schools extra pay, allowances, housing assistance, and transport aid — a recognition of their service in communities far from urban centers.

Yu emphasized that the measure requires inter-agency cooperation, with the Department of Education leading implementation, the Department of Public Works and Highways building access roads, the Department of Energy providing electricity, and the Department of Information and Communications Technology ensuring connectivity.

Article continues after this 

For Zamboanga del Sur, where indigenous communities and rural families live in some of the most difficut terrains, the law is expected to be transformative.

Yu said the measure is “one big step in our mission to provide an accessible means of achieving progress, including ones as basic as getting the first formative education.”

Article continues after this 

With RA 12321 now enacted, classrooms are set to rise in sitios long deprived of learning facilities, offering hope that children in Zamboanga del Sur will no longer have to endure exhausting journeys just to study, according to Yu. /apl

World.title: PCSO rolls out relief operations for flood-hit Davao City
World.content:
The Philippine Sweepstakes Charity Office augments its relief operations by tapping its Authorized Agent Corporations. —Photo from the PCSO

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO), following the directive of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., immediately mobilized its relief operations on Saturday in several areas hit by flash floods in Davao City.

Less than a day after the flooding, the PCSO activated its quick response mechanism by directing its regional branches to coordinate relief efforts on the ground, while tapping its network of Authorized Agent Corporations (AACs) to augment the agency’s relief operations.

Among the first to respond were Hexaprime Inc., Magic Three Gaming Corp., Northman Gaming Corp., and Antiguas Gaming Corp., with other AACs expected to extend support as relief efforts continue.

Article continues after this 

READ: PCSO completes historic 100% nationwide PTV rollout

The flash floods hit Davao City on Friday, July 24, after heavy rains triggered by the southwest monsoon caused rivers and waterways to overflow, affecting thousands of residents and prompting emergency response operations.

According to PCSO General Manager Melquiades A. Robles, the agency wasted no time in deploying assistance.

“Time is of the essence during calamities. Every hour counts in bringing much-needed assistance to affected families,” Robles said. “Through the immediate mobilization of our regional offices and the invaluable support of our Authorized Agent Corporations, we are able to respond swiftly and extend help where it is needed most.”

The immediate relief operations are in line with the president’s directive for government agencies to ensure prompt and efficient delivery of services during emergencies.

Article continues after this 

READ: Pagcor, PCSO open to budget realignment for crisis funding

According to Robles, the PCSO’s extensive network of regional branches and private-sector partners enables it to respond quickly to emergencies in various part of the country, allowing relief goods to be mobilized and distributed without delay.

Article continues after this 

“The PCSO remains steadfast in its commitment to serve the Filipino people, especially during times of crisis. We will continue working with our regional offices, local government units, and partner organizations to ensure that assistance reaches our affected kababayans as quickly as possible,” Robles said.

The PCSO said it continues to monitor the situation in Davao City and stands ready to provide additional assistance as needed, in coordination with local authorities and other government agencies. /atm

World.title: House to prioritize passage of remaining 26 priority admin bills
World.content:
House of Representatives. Inquirer file photo

MANILA, Philippines — The House of Representatives is committed to prioritizing the approval of the remaining 26 out of 52 priority administration bills, Majority Leader Ferdinand Alexander “Sandro” A. Marcos said in a statement on Sunday.

“We have so far passed 26 measures, or half of our target, during the First Regular Session of the 20th Congress. We will work on approving the rest in the course of our Second Regular Session,” he said.

According to him, priority bills agreed earlier between the legislative and executive branches in the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council (Ledac) contain structural reforms that would support the programs of President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. and “help our people as well.”

Article continues after this 

“We will make sure that this proposed law will help our president, and especially our people in making their lives more comfortable,” the majority leader stressed.

READ: SONA 2026: Marcos enters final two years with key bills pending

He also pointed out that other priority measures, like the proposed amendments to the Universal Health Care Act, would benefit the people in general.

They also aim to streamline the implementation of these laws so the people can easily access the programs and benefits Congress has provided for them in these pieces of legislation, he added.

He said other bills are targeted at specific sectors, such as proposed changes in the Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund Act and in the Magna Carta for Small and Medium-Scale Enterprises.

Article continues after this 

“Our country should receive and feel the benefits set aside for them under our laws,” Marcos.

He noted that other pending measures seek to promote transparency and good governance, such as the proposed amendments to the Bank Secrecy Law and Anti-Money Laundering Act.

Article continues after this 

A status report released by the House Committee on Rules, which Marcos heads, shows the 26 priority bills that have been passed by the House include the proposal to reset the first regular elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), which has been enacted into law.

World.title: Marcos’ 5th Sona should go beyond promises – Villanueva
World.content:
A delivery rider drives past an official State of the Nation Address banner near the House of Representatives in Quezon City on Sunday, July 26, 2026. (Photo by GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE / INQUIRER.net)

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Joel Villanueva on Sunday said this year’s state of the nation address (Sona) should present a clear roadmap that delivers quality jobs, better education and a solution to widespread hunger.

Villanueva made the pronouncement as President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is set to deliver his fifth Sona on Monday, July 27.

READ: Sona 2026 – Inquirer.net

Article continues after this 

“This year’s Sona must answer the questions that matter most to ordinary Filipinos: Where are the jobs? How will families put food on the table? How will we reduce poverty? How do we give our children a better future through education?” Villanueva asked in a statement.

According to Villanueva, the president must address these issues as Filipinos continue to grapple with rising costs and unemployment, leading to economic uncertainty.

The unemployment rate in the country, as of May 2026, currently sits 4.8 percent, reflecting 2.5 million jobless Filipinos.

The underemployment rate, on the other hand, is at 12.2 percent—equivalent to 6.04 million Filipinos who seek more hours of work or an extra job.

Results of a March 2026 Social Weather Stations survey also showed an uptick in the country’s hunger incidence rate, now at 23.2 percent, higher than 20.1 percent in November 2025.

Article continues after this 

Inflation, meanwhile, is at 6.4 percent in June 2026, way higher compared to 1.4 percent in June 2025.

The senator also cited challenges in education – from low literacy rate, lack of classrooms and low Math and reading proficiency to rising school violence as seen in recent shootings.

Article continues after this 

“Real challenges call for real action. The nation’s biggest problems can’t wait,” Villanueva said.

“The best anti-poverty program is a decent job. The best way to fight hunger is to ensure that every Filipino who wants to work has access to job opportunities,” he noted.

He added: “At the end of the day, the measure of any Sona is simple: Will it bring more jobs, put food on the table, and give every Filipino child a better future?” /apl

World.title: Groups call out anti-disinfo bills giving gov’t power to take down social media posts
World.content:
An illustration shows a scammer in a hoodie working on a computer. —Image by Dannie Agacer

MANILA, Philippines — A broad front of journalists, academics, civil society groups, and professionals is forming to oppose proposed legislation on disinformation. They say that efforts to curb disinformation on social media could end up worsening the problem rather than solving it.

On the weekend before President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s penultimate State of the Nation Address (Sona) before Congress, about 50 journalists, tech and related companies and advocacies, the academe, and civil society gathered Saturday, July 25, at the University of the Philippines’ College of Media and Communication to line up action plans to oppose the legislation which, at the current form, includes imprisonment and government takedown powers of social media posts, roundtable discussion organizers said.

House Bill No. 9465, authored by Ilocos Sur Rep. Sandro Marcos and several others, is awaiting movement of the counterpart proposal in the Senate, which held a hearing on Feb. 11, 2026, under the Committee on Media and Information, then chaired by Sen. Robinhood Padilla.

Article continues after this 

Dean Diosa Labiste (right) of the University of the Philippines’ College of Media and Communication welcomes participants of a roundtable discussion fleshing out the alleged dangers of proposed legislation to fight disinformation. —Photo by Arlene Burgos | INQUIRER.net

The anti-disinformation bill is in the older Marcos’ legislative agenda, as one of the priority bills endorsed for passage by June 2026 by the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council (Ledac).

Carlo Nazareno of Democracy.net.ph, which has been actively engaging with Congress on the anti-false information legislation at the House of Representatives, said the bill includes harsh penalties, such as six to 12 years of prison time.

“If the accused is a media personality, it is considered an aggravating circumstance, which entails increased penalties, potentially leading to a chilling effect for journalists. While the lower house bill takes many cues from the European Union’s Digital Services Act, which seeks to hold platforms to account, a provision was inserted which gives platforms a liability shield, which runs counter to the DSA,” Nazareno said.

The Senate version of the bill establishes the creation of a Digital Media Integrity Council, composed of agencies mostly from the executive branch, media organizations, and online intermediaries. It is given internet content takedown powers, a function that the Supreme Court ruled requires a court order, he said.

Both Democracy.net.ph and the SIGLA Research Center, which organized Saturday’s roundtable, said they recognize the urgency of acting against disinformation, but cautioned against certain provisions of existing draft laws. They said that this potentially may be a case of the supposed cure worsening the disease.

Article continues after this 

“This is by no means a minimization of the harms that it causes, because among our ranks, you have people that see most palpably the harms that are caused by disinformation… But we realize that the costs far outweigh the benefits,” said Justin Felip Daduya of SIGLA.

“The threat to our digital rights, to our right to speech, it’s not worth a bill, especially if it can’t address the crisis in the first place… It settles for low-hanging fruit, but it leaves the roots of the disinformation crisis unscathed,” Daduya said in a mix of Filipino and English.

Article continues after this 

Many of Saturday’s attendees were from the groups that have issued two public statements on why they find the proposals objectionable.

Together, the two statements say the pending pieces of legislation are problematic because these punish individual expression and target individual social media users while failing to hold to account the actual disinformation architects or the social media platforms.

They also take exception to “takedown provisions,” calling these a reactive approach that risks censorship and calls on the power of the state to be the “arbiter of truth” because government units may be tasked to filter content and tag it.

Anti-disinformation bill position

Public statement on the anti-disinformation bill

The ‘Robin’ factor

The Committee on Public Information and Mass Media in the Senate conducted a hearing in February on the disinformation bills — Anti-False Content and Fake News Act, Social Media Transparency Act, Anti-Troll Farm Act, and related social-media safety bills.

It is not yet known if Padilla remains chair of said committee after the chamber’s leadership change and reorganization in June 2026.

READ: New Senate committee chairpersons named amid shake-up

Several roundtable participants Saturday expressed worry that apart from the specific provisions that are feared to stifle dissent or endanger protected speech in the name of curbing disinformation, having Padilla at the helm of the Senate panel tackling the disinformation bills may pose a problem given his political leanings and appreciation of the issues.

There are at least two Senate proposals that may be included in the discussions: the Social Media and Fairness and Algorithmic Transparency Act of 2025 by former Senate President Vicente Sotto III, and the Anti-Troll Farm Act by Padilla.

Proposed Social Media Fairness and Algorithmic Transparency Act of 2025

‘Does not punish dissent’

House Speaker Faustino Dy III said last month that HB 9465 was carefully crafted to protect constitutional freedoms.

The House website also said their bill “sets a high threshold for criminal liability and expressly protects political opinions, criticism of government and public officials, satire, journalism, whistleblowing, academic discourse, artistic expression and religious expression.”

The measure, it was said, requires digital platforms operating in the Philippines to establish a legal presence in the country and comply with transparency, disclosure and user protection standards.

READ: House approves anti-fake news bill on final reading

Continuing legislative process

Former Gabriela party-list Rep. Arlene Brosas, now co-chairperson of Makabayan group, said she expects government to push for the immediate enactment of the disinformation proposals. She clarified that bills proposed by the end of the First Regular Session of the 20th Congress will be carried and would continue to be processed in the Congress resumption of session tomorrow.

Brosas said terms and concepts in the House version, such as reckless disregard, verifiable public harm, and serious threat to national security, are open to interpretation, “potentially allowing inconsistent or politically motivated enforcement.”

“There is a possibility that activists or individuals sharing politically sensitive posts could be subjected to red tagging or politically motivated prosecution before courts ultimately dismiss the cases. The bill does not sufficiently guarantee the independence of accredited researchers and fact-checkers,” she said.
