World.title: ‘Dead in the water’: Navy’s flagship ‘drone ship’ program in doubt
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalDefence ‘Dead in the water’: Navy’s flagship ‘drone ship’ program in doubt Matthew Knott July 26, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A centrepiece of the Albanese government’s push to modernise the navy – a fleet of large, heavily armed warships that can operate with or without sailors on board – has been thrown into doubt after the United States military dumped its plan to develop the vessels. The government insists it is committed to the vision outlined in its 2024 surface fleet review, but defence experts say they expect the plan will need to be abandoned or overhauled. The government announced with much fanfare two years ago that it would boost the firepower of the navy by acquiring six large optionally crewed surface vessels packed with missiles and based on a prototype being developed in the US. A US naval vessel, USV Ranger, on the Pacific Ocean during a training exercise in 2023. But the US navy last year scrapped that program and is instead pursuing a fleet of smaller drone ships that do not have the option of crew members.



Richard Dunley, a senior lecturer in maritime strategy at UNSW, said the US navy’s large unmanned surface vessel program “has been killed”, raising serious questions about the future of Australia’s plan. “The universal assumption was that Australia would piggyback off the US vessel,” he said. “I find it very difficult to see how Australia could do this on our own. “I keep expecting to hear that it’s dead, and I was surprised to see it feature in this year’s national defence strategy.” Former naval officer Jennifer Parker, an expert associate at the Australian National University’s national security college, agreed, saying: “I think we will end up abandoning the idea of large optionally crewed vessels and move to unmanned medium-sized surface vessels in line with the US.”



The vessels would also probably use containerised weapons rather than the vertical launch system envisaged under the government’s plan, she said. The government allocated up to $300 million for optionally crewed surface vessels in its 10-year defence spending plan released in April. But with the vessels estimated to cost around $US250 million ($360 million) each to build, the total cost of the program would ultimately be billions of dollars. Related Article Defence Why the navy is buying a ghost fleet of drone boats for ‘three D’ jobs: Dirty, dull or dangerous “The government is investing $52-$65 billion over the decade to deliver a larger, more lethal surface combatant fleet, through enhancements to strike, air defence and undersea warfare capabilities including six large optionally crewed surface vessels with up to 32 vertical launch system cells to increase the ADF’s maritime long-range strike capability,” a Defence spokesperson said. Greens defence spokesman David Shoebridge called for the government to admit it was proposing to buy a “ghost ship”, describing the affair as the “perfect example of what is wrong with Defence right now.



“The US had a thought-bubble about an experimental and boutique military asset and Labor and the Coalition was so desperate to show their loyalty to the US they immediately signed us up,” he said. “Then when the US spiked the program, without ever consulting Australia, we are left with $300 million attached to a project that is dead in the water. “It’s not just the embarrassment and the incompetence, there is also a huge opportunity cost here in terms of public money and defence resources.” Kamikaze drone boats have played a crucial role in the war in Iran, but these are far smaller and more expendable than the large arsenal ships Australia plans to acquire. Defence firm Austal in November unveiled designs for two new optionally crewed surface vessels – known as the Vantage-class – which it said could meet the Australian navy’s needs.



But military leaders have said they remain committed to developing the vessels with the US. “There is an opportunity for us to realise a really important capability that would take our fleet forwards in terms of its lethality and survivability, but that can’t happen if the US navy don’t commit to the program,” Defence Force vice chief Robert Chipman told Senate estimates hearings in June. “It was tied to the US navy, and there are currently no other options that we’re considering.” Chipman added: “We recognise that there are potential delays to the large optionally crewed vessel, so, yes, we are tracking what the US Navy is saying.” The surface fleet review said the navy would acquire the six vessels “through formal engagement with the United States Navy program as a fast follower”, with an expectation they would enter service in the 2030s and 2040s.



Defence Minister Richard Marles said at the time the vessels would be “exactly based on what has been developed in the United States”, describing the prototype as a “known quantity”. “They have the capacity to operate in an uncrewed fashion, but it is the intention of the Royal Australian Navy to crew these vessels,” he said. Dunley warned at the time that the government was gambling on unproven technology and that the vessels had critics within the US navy. Rear Admiral William Daly, the US navy’s surface warfare requirements director, said last year the large vessels had “walked the path towards exquisite, expensive [and] unpalatable”. The US Naval Institute reported last year that the US military was moving away from optionally crewed vessels because they are considered too costly and complicated.



Unmanned vessels do not require berthing space, galleys, toilets and other features needed to support sailors on board. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Five Liberal MPs supported a factional deal. Now it’s at the centre of a corruption probe
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWOperation Rosny Five Liberal MPs supported a factional deal. Now it’s at the centre of a corruption probe Michael McGowan July 26, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Five current NSW Liberal MPs voted for a factional deal to replace sitting members of the Hills Shire Council while they were on the party’s powerful state executive – a decision likely to be central to an anti-corruption probe into fugitive property developer Jean Nassif’s links to Liberal powerbrokers. Ahead of the launch of the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s Operation Rosny inquiry on Monday, the Herald has obtained documents from the October 2021 meeting of the Liberal state executive at which members voted to install new council candidates in The Hills. The eight-week ICAC inquiry into the fugitive property developer Jean Nassif’s links to Liberal powerbrokers will begin on Monday. Michael Howard The vote helped spark the ICAC’s probe, after Kellyville MP Ray Williams made an explosive speech to parliament in mid-2022 alleging Nassif had paid “significant funds” to Liberal Party apparatchik Christian Ellis and other senior party members to install new councillors in The Hills Shire Council who would support Nassif’s future development applications. Then-Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet referred Williams’ claims to the ICAC the following day.



Related Article Exclusive

Operation Rosny Revealed: First witnesses to front sensational corruption investigation The documents obtained by the Herald confirm for the first time the details of the decision to bypass a preselection and install new councillors. The motion, authored by then NSW Liberal president Philip Ruddock, states he had been advised of an “agreed position with respect to selecting and endorsing candidates for the 2021 local government elections in The Hills local government area”. Some of the candidates, the document noted, had not been vetted, while others “did not originally nominate for these positions”. Voting records for the meeting show while he is listed as the author of the motion, Ruddock himself abstained from voting. Asked why by the Herald, the former attorney-general said: “I have no recollection of those matters.”



But five current MPs who were on the state executive at the time supported it. The group includes four current members of Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane’s frontbench: Chris Rath, James Wallace, Jacqui Munro and Mark Coure. All four are from the dominant moderate faction. The fifth is upper house MP Aileen MacDonald. NSW Liberal MP Chris Rath. Oscar Colman The five MPs either declined to comment or did not respond to questions by the Herald. There is no suggestion any of the five MPs were aware of the allegations surrounding the vote at the time. Instead, senior moderate sources said the vote was part of what had been a long-running agreement between the hard-right and moderate factions that emerged out of the agreement between senior NSW Liberals Matt Kean and Dominic Perrottet.



Related Article Exclusive

Operation Rosny The Liberals’ sliding doors moment that led to a blockbuster ICAC inquiry “As far as we were concerned, it was factional politics as usual in a part of the world that was always really brutal,” one senior moderate who asked to speak on the condition of anonymity to discuss an internal party matter said. However, many Liberal MPs are privately resigned to the likelihood that the eight-week ICAC inquiry will draw in multiple members of Sloane’s opposition. Although no MPs have been accused of any wrongdoing, the inquiry has the potential to be hugely damaging for the party even by dragging out a period of messy internal factionalism. At the same time, senior party members had long raised concerns about Ellis, and his links to Nassif, before the Hills vote.



The Herald has previously revealed senior party members had unsuccessfully sought to stop Ellis’s ascension to the party’s state executive as far back as 2019 because of his links to lobbying firm Beckington. Toplace, Nassif’s company, was registered as a client of Beckington’s from July 2020. Before his speech to parliament in 2022, Ray Williams, who is a member of the centre-right faction, also raised concerns with then-premier Gladys Berejiklian as early as November 2020. Ray Williams is the Liberal MP for Kellyville. Wolter Peeters In a series of text messages, first reported by the ABC and confirmed by the Herald, Williams wrote to Berejiklian urging her to help block attempts by the right faction to move three party branches into the Hills Shire in a bid to control council preselections there. “It’s completely uncalled for and just an attempt to put [councillors] into the Hills Council who support a particular developer,” Williams wrote at the time, referring to Nassif.



“Raymondo, I’ll call you first thing in the morning Darl,” Berejiklian replied. Berejiklian initially told Williams she and the then-police minister David Elliott, also a member of the centre-right, were “trying to calm the troops and delay”, but that “so far no one is budging”. After Williams sent a series of further entreaties, he texted the premier again on the day of the ballot asking whether her representative on the state executive would abstain from the vote. “I’m not getting involved in this Ray,” she wrote back. “I’m sick of everyone trying to embroil me in factional issues. I have too much on my plate.”



When Williams said it was “much bigger than factionalism” and involved “corruption by a few on state executive”, Berejiklian said: “You need to report it”. “I certainly am,” Williams replied. “Good!!” Berejiklian said. Ellis is one of 10 persons of interest before the ICAC as part of Operation Rosny, its wide-ranging probe into Nassif’s links to party powerbrokers, councils and the state’s Catholic schools. The first witness before the public inquiry on Monday will be Michael O’Hara, a publican, lawyer and developer who is a focus of the ICAC’s inquiry. Dylan Whitelaw, a one-time Liberal staffer who has previously been closely associated with many of the figures central to the inquiry, will appear on Tuesday. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: How about the 34-year-old who out-scored Essendon on Saturday
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 How about the 34-year-old who out-scored Essendon on Saturday Peter Ryan July 26, 2026 — 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points The AFL has 112 listed players in their 30s. A decade ago it was only 65.

Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera has done it again in July.

‘F--- off’ should not be the phrase of choice between Suns teammates.

Carlton’s Lewis Young went back on his mark further than Michael Holding.

Jack Gunston’s seven-goal haul against Essendon helped the cause of veterans wanting to play on in 2027. He is 34, has kicked 100 goals in his past 30 matches, and kicked a matchwinning behind for the Hawks on Easter Monday against Geelong. He has now kicked five bags of five goals this season. According to @sirswampthing he became the third-oldest player to outscore the opposition with his 7.2 (44) topping the Bombers 5.9 (39) on Saturday. Hawthorn star Jack Gunston kicked his 600th goal during a brilliant third quarter. AFL Photos via Getty Images



His performance was a timely reminder of the increased presence and influence of older players in the competition in the same week he and 36-year-old Cat Patrick Dangerfield signed on for another season. Unusually, the trend has become the old-timer’s friend. It’s no longer unusual to have at least half a dozen players on a club list who are 30-something. In 2026, there were 112 listed players still getting dirty in their 30s. In 2016, there were only 65. In 2026, eight players of the top 20 highest rating players in the competition are 30-something. In 2016, the only player was then Suns’ champion Gary Ablett jr. Four of the top players in this year’s coaches’ votes are in their 30s right now. In 2016 there were zero.



The shift has not just occurred because the money is too good to pass up and sports science has improved player longevity. Games record holder and the oldest player in the game Scott Pendlebury makes a huge contribution to the Magpies AFL Photos Clubs now recognise how valuable it can be to have older players on their list as long as they fill a few preconditions. They need to lose the grumpy pills which are allocated to everyone in greater numbers after each year after they reach 30. That means accepting a different role which may mean playing out of the midfield, or less game time, or fewer games, or even playing VFL and accepting the importance and satisfaction of the often underappreciated teaching job.



The AFL’s oldest current players 38 Scott Pendlebury (Collingwood)

37 Dayne Zorko (Brisbane Lions)

36 Patrick Dangerfield (Geelong)*

36 Taylor Walker (Adelaide)

36 Dane Rampe (Sydney Swans)

36 Jeremy Howe (Collingwood)

35 Steele Sidebottom (Collingwood)

35 Rhys Stanley (Geelong)

35 Mason Cox (Fremantle)

34 Mark Blicavs (Geelong)

34 Jake Melksham (Melbourne)

34 Jack Gunston (Hawthorn)*

34 Max Gawn (Melbourne)*

34 Nick Haynes (Carlton)

34 Tom Liberatore (Western Bulldogs) Of the top 15 oldest players in the league, only Melbourne’s Max Gawn has played every match and remains at his peak every match. The rest have accepted something different. Even Gawn has pulled back a little to give Max Heath a taste when possible. Resisting the temptation to be grumpy means taking notice of players and people in the program, passing on wisdom and enjoying the achievements of those many years your junior. You can set some people straight or you can expand your own sense of what is possible and gain a new lease of life. Anyone who saw teammates celebrate the 600th career goal of the friendly curmudgeon that is Gunston by making him the centre of attention understood how great clubs are built on connections between generations. To play on, a player needs to maintain their weapons so they can be deployed in a role that suits the team’s needs – if not every match then often enough.



The skipper Patrick Dangerfield will play on in 2027 Getty Images Dangerfield’s power remains although it’s used to win or halve contests inside 50 rather than in the midfield where he would need to work too hard to stay in the game. Scott Pendlebury’s poise and ability to put teammates into space is a feature, Jeremy Howe’s leap and defensive know-how is strong, Dayne Zorko hasn’t lost his pace or capacity to kick darts. In an excellent piece of coaching, Gunston has had a role created for him inside 50 which suits his strengths. The disconnected forward leads hard and is an accurate set shot. It’s not easy but certainly his workload is less than others. Imagine what Ben King will learn from him next season? They are no longer their club’s best players – although they can be the best man on the ground in a quarter or half occasionally as Gunston was in the third quarter on Saturday – but the team is better for their presence.



Clubs have also decided a veteran who can play can add depth to their list and complement their team in a way a mediocre mid-20s player can’t. It’s why free agency has proved a bigger boon for strong teams than weaker ones (Good old Lachie Neale forever?). They can add quality players who increase competition for spots, add poise and experience and therefore valuable lessons to both AFL and VFL teams, and during the week when clubs undergo situational training their input is useful. It’s recognition of a point champion cricketer Greg Chappell made in his book Not Out - accepted wisdom among coaches without ego - that players learn better from their peers than coaches. There is also an in-built resilience in veterans as they navigate a long season under scrutiny with all sorts of ups and downs that helps younger players find perspective when challenges inevitably arise.



The extra man on the bench has also given an impetus to the clubs’ willingness to retain veterans as they can manage their time better and have more options when planning how they are going to cover roles. Going on might be good for Gunston and his peers, but this situation has not arisen because clubs have suddenly become generous. The times they are a-changin’ and the veterans’ importance will be on display in September when they challenge the relatively inexperienced premiership favourite Fremantle.



Nasiah the messiah should get the three votes Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera defeated the Kangaroos to keep the Saints’ wildcard chances alive. He charged into the game like a fire truck scattering traffic when he kicked three goals and created another goal for Darcy Wilson after chasing down Finn O’Sullivan in the third quarter. Not only did his sheer brilliance shift the contest, his presence lifted teammates and signalled a return to form after he lost his way against the close checking Cat in round 19. He became the first player to reach 30 disposals, gain 750 metres and kick three goals in the first three quarters. Then he kicked the Saints’ first goal of the final quarter with a steal from Caleb Daniel that ended with a running banana.



View post on X The performance was a reprise of his memorable two-vote winning effort against Melbourne on July 27 last season (it was July 26 on Sunday) and a reminder of the reason the Saints paid such a large percentage of their salary cap this season to keep him. Does he get changed in a phone box before games at this time of the year? Thankfully, the umpires have the statistics on hand when voting for the Brownlow. Surely 46 touches (even allowing for kick-ins), four goals, and five clearances will earn him BOG honours. For the Suns, it’s a season not to forget



‘F--- off’ should not be the phrase of choice between Suns’ teammates given the unfortunate pattern of players taking the direction literally. That teenager Leo Lombard chose to direct that response to animated feedback from a frustrated veteran Christian Petracca is not ideal but it can be easily addressed. It’s not uncommon for interactions between teammates to get off track midway through games. Leo Lombard looks on after a spray from Christian Petracca. Fox Footy The problem for the Suns is that it reinforces the sense among other clubs that Suns’ players argue on field more than other teams in 2026 (officials at two clubs had mentioned this Suns’ characteristic to this column in the past few months). It also symbolises a season that has spun out of control since their win over Port Adelaide in round 10 in Darwin, when they sat fourth on the ladder and Ben King indicated he wanted to stay at the club.



No doubt they have unravelled, but a more in-depth look at their performances indicates more lies behind the drop-off than suggestions of discord, of which there have been plenty, all denied by the Suns. In those first 10 matches, they beat an underdone Geelong, followed by wins over battlers West Coast, Richmond, Essendon, Giants, St Kilda and Port Adelaide. Since Darwin they ran out of legs against North Melbourne then have lost to Brisbane, Geelong, Hawthorn, Fremantle, Collingwood, Adelaide, Western Bulldogs and now Carlton. That’s like a racehorse being found wanting when stepping up to the wrong grade. Add other elements and a clear picture emerges than the shadow the Suns are casting right now.



Injury has ruined Matt Rowell’s year, Mac Andrew’s development has been slow, the ruck rules have pushed Jarrod Witts off the cliff, Bailey Humphrey became distracted by trade talk, and Ben Ainsworth, Sam Flanders, Brayden Fiorini, Connor Budarick and David Swallow all exited after playing in the winning final and were replaced with more talented but less ready players such as Lombard. The other - more existential issue - is that problems of retention have not been solved with Rowell the next contract discussion to be had. And their team needs to deal with frustration better and bounce back from disappointment. That is something they can’t stick their head in the Surfers Paradise sand and hide from. Smart play young man Carlton’s Lewis Young consoles his Suns’ opponent Ned Moyle AFL Photos



Carlton’s Lewis Young went back on his mark further than Michael Holding on his run-up when he had a set shot late in the game against Gold Coast. He not only used the 30 seconds available for players taking a set shot but by taking the Ben Brown run up was able to drain another 14 seconds off the clock during his run-up before kicking. The time remaining went from 3.48 to 3.04 minutes left in the game. It will be interesting if someone tries the same [long] approach in finals. Later that night, Richmond’s Luke Trainor kicked the ball out on the full from outside the boundary line after receiving a free kick for out on the full. However, because he had not returned into play the ball was brought back to where he kicked it for a boundary throw-in. It was a strange rule anomaly that requires consideration post-season. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘We stand by our decision to play him’: Lyon feels the heat after King’s AFL comeback ends early
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘We stand by our decision to play him’: Lyon feels the heat after King’s AFL comeback ends early Marc McGowan Updated July 26, 2026 — 9:48pm ,first published 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

St Kilda coach Ross Lyon is adamant tortured St Kilda spearhead Max King was ready to play on Sunday despite his first AFL game in 757 days ending prematurely due to hamstring tightness. King’s latest setback in a challenging period for the 26-year-old marred the Saints’ 31-point win over fellow wildcard contender North Melbourne at Marvel Stadium, including a four-goal-to-one final quarter that transformed a competitive contest into a comfortable victory. Max King in full flight during Sunday’s match. AFL Photos via Getty Images Resident superstar Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera was the difference again, kicking three of his four goals after going forward in the third quarter as part of a 46-disposal performance that ripped the match away from the Kangaroos. Lyon did not speak to King before his post-game media conference, but said that the star forward would undergo scans on Monday to assess any potential damage. The coach backed his medical staff’s decision to give King the green light after he suffered a hamstring strain in a VFL game in May.



Related Article Investigation

AFL off-field behaviour Crime threats, nude pics and a Tinder date: Inside the AFL’s most secretive unit “I don’t even know what the outcome is, so how can it be an error before there’s an outcome?” Lyon said. “But we stand by our decision to play him. We have high-performance experts, we have [training] load, we have conditioning. We’re really quite confident. “In the four-week [rehabilitation] block, he had 50 per cent more volume of high-speed running, and 500 per cent more very high-speed running, which is above 24 kilometres [an hour]. His biggest sessions were game-load sessions with 20 per cent more. “So, in the context of that evidence, our conditioners thought [he was ready], and game time was only 12 minutes a quarter – two six-minute stints. It was very considered, very worked out, and I’m happy for it to sit with me and our team because we collaborate.”



King had just one kick – a long set shot from the boundary in the second quarter – and one handball in limited game time, but left the ground for good only 13 minutes into the third term. He went to the rooms soon after and did not reappear before the Saints ruled him out. King’s hamstring strain in May added to the knee and calf setbacks which stalled a promising career that was stuck on 83 games for more than two years. Speaking post-match to SEN, St Kilda veteran Brad Hill was hopeful King had avoided another lengthy lay-off. Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera, being embraced by teammate Liam Ryan, was the match-winner for St Kilda. AFL Photos via Getty Images



“Fingers crossed because if it is [serious], it’s so sad,” Hill said. “It’s been a tough journey for him the last couple of years, so I’m hoping nothing bad has happened.” King started every quarter on the bench and came on after the seven-minute mark each time. North Melbourne defenders Charlie Comben and Aidan Corr took turns playing on him, and rarely afforded him much space. His most notable impact was a forceful collision with Cam Zurhaar that cost the big Saint a 50-metre penalty after the Kangaroo reeled in an intercept mark. King’s nightmare period started with a season-ending posterior cruciate ligament tear in his left knee in a two-point loss to Port Adelaide at Marvel Stadium on June 30, 2024. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Of course we can win it’: Defiant Dangerfield backs the Cats to contend again, despite his injury



He signed a six-year contract extension in October that year to tie him to the Saints until 2032, but has endured repeated injury complications since, including three surgeries on his right knee last year after a pre-season setback. King’s trouble continued with a calf injury in February before the hamstring strain in his second VFL match of the season in May delayed his return further. He spent part of his latest rehabilitation block on the Gold Coast, enabling him to spend time with his twin Ben, and St Kilda opted to bring him straight into the senior side. “It’s not ideal, right? But it’s about resilience and coming again,” Lyon said. “I think ultimately, you go, ‘Geez, I’ve run down the AFL race, I feel good, had a start, got a feel for how hard it is, and [I will] rehab a potential soft tissue’. Who knows what it is? I don’t know.



The Saints also lost Cooper Sharman (managed) and Rowan Marshall (back spasms) as late withdrawals, the latter after completing the warm-up. King could be facing another stint on the sidelines. AFL Photos via Getty Images Dashers Hill (34 disposals) and Darcy Wilson (28) were other prominent players for St Kilda, while ruckman Tom De Koning (19, seven clearances) shone in his return from broken ribs and a punctured lung. They led by 16 points at quarter-time – benefiting from a series of wayward North Melbourne set shots – but the Roos hit the front early in the second half via the second of Jack Darling’s three goals. But thanks to their 41-23 clearance dominance, the 10th-placed Saints hit back to lead by 13 points at the final break before kicking away for an important triumph.



Kangaroos defender Charlie Comben went to hospital after he was coughing up blood from a heavy collision late in the match, but coach Alastair Clarkson said the club’s doctors were optimistic he had avoided a serious issue.

World.title: The two women that sealed Lomax’s lucrative, three-year NRL return
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The two women that sealed Lomax’s lucrative, three-year NRL return Dan Walsh July 26, 2026 — 9:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Zac Lomax says the “chance to be part of history” and his partner’s approval to raise their first child in the PNG Chiefs’ confined resort-style accommodation sealed his return to rugby league on a lucrative three-year deal. Lomax was unveiled as the Chiefs fifth signing for 2028 on Sunday afternoon at a local match in Port Moresby, which he attended alongside club officials and Prime Minister James Marape. Loading The 26-year-old’s deal is estimated to be worth between $700-800,000 per season and is tax-exempt under the Australian-PNG government agreement on player salaries at the incoming franchise. The Chiefs recruitment coup will bring Lomax back to the NRL after next year’s Rugby World Cup, with Lomax briefly addressing his code-hopping in a hastily arranged press conference with local media.



“Obviously I didn’t think [a rugby league] return was going to be too soon,” Lomax said. “But life changes and circumstances do and it’s all for the better. Everything happens for a reason and you go with it… I’m all in and [the Chiefs move] is obviously in 2028. In regards to rugby I’m still still there for another year. Zac Lomax’s return to the NRL is now official. Getty Images “I’m really looking forward to finishing that the best that I can and and competing there the best I can.” Lomax’s move to rugby on a two-year Western Force deal, after going all-in on the breakaway R360 competition, amounted to an estimated $350,000-a-year shortfall from his previous Parramatta contract.



Fellow Chiefs target Joey Manu is weighing up a multi-year offer of his own after touring PNG’s housing and club facilities last week. Manu has another year to run on his $1.6 million Racing 92 contract, but he has already been offered to rival NRL clubs as a potential mid-season signing next year before potentially linking with the Chiefs in 2028. Former Rooster Joey Manu and his family at Port Moresby airport on Monday. Lomax and his family were sold on the move once his partner Kayla and mum Cheree agreed that the Chiefs five-star accommodation facilities would be suitable for their first child, expected early next year. “To come over here and have my family experience it, that was probably the main thing that was the ticket of approval,” Lomax said.



“We’ve got a little baby on the way so that was the thing that we really had to look at. But [Chiefs CEO] Lorna [McPherson], she’s like another mum. “I think I knew – to be a part of history is what I was leaning towards straight away. And when I first caught up with [PNG officials] it was about leaving a legacy, changing the nation and just giving back to the country”. Lomax joins marquee half Jarome Luai, Souths veteran winger Alex Johnston, NSW Origin utility Connor Watson and English international Matty Lees as PNG’s confirmed 2028 signings. PNG internationals Gairo Voro, Morea Morea and Finley Glare are also on the books on two-year development deals. The Chiefs tax-free exemptions and marquee signings have put rival NRL clubs on high-alert and privately bemoaning a player market that has been turned on its head by the new franchise.



November 1 – when PNG can formally talk to any player coming off-contract in 2027 – now looms larger than ever in the scramble for topline talent, as Chiefs general manager Michael Chammas pointed to the knock-on effect of signings like Lomax. Related Article NRL 2026 Has Adam Doueihi played his last game for Wests Tigers? “We’re three months away from that November 1 free agency and no one really expected us to have many players signed by the time we got there,” Chammas said. “It’s exciting. You go to players on November 1 and say ‘hey, do you want to play with these guys?’ and I think it’s a lot more appealing doing that than going there without anyone signed. “So hopefully there’s a few more before November 1 and we’ll start to assemble quite a competitive roster”.
